hook: You know this verse from a number one hit song. But did you know the poem is followed by a question about what profit a worker really has?
story:
Fourteen pairs. Count them in the verses that follow and there are fourteen: a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to pluck up, a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time for war and a time for peace. Twenty-eight times the word comes round, and every one of them is set against its opposite. The whole of human life is laid out in two columns, and nothing is left off either side.

Then, by most accounts around the end of the 1950s, a folk singer found the poem. Pete Seeger was angry at his publisher, who had told him he could not sell the protest songs Seeger wrote. By his own account he pulled a slip of paper out of his pocket and set the old words to a melody in about fifteen minutes. He added only a few words of his own, the title phrase and a closing line. The publisher wrote back with enthusiasm, and within two months had sold the song on. Seeger recorded a demo around 1961, and a live version appeared on his 1962 album The Bitter and the Sweet.

In late 1965 The Byrds plugged it in. Their single spent three weeks at number one, as the Vietnam War was just beginning. A poem about a time for war and a time for peace, written long before anyone sang it, was suddenly on the radio across America. Seeger, for his part, liked their version, and said the guitars sounded like bells.

So the verse you may know from a record is the opening line of something older and stranger than the record. It is the first line of a poem that sits inside a book whose Preacher asks in its first chapter what a person gains from all labor under the sun.

sources.title: Far Out Magazine: The biblical inspiration behind one of The Byrds’ greatest songs
Stereogum, The Number Ones: The Byrds, Turn! Turn! Turn!

moment:
The poem is not a prayer or a command. It is a list. Nothing in it says what a person must do. It says that there is a season for each thing, and the next lines turn straight to a question: “What profit has he who works in that in which he labors?” The Preacher goes on, “I have seen the burden which God has given to the sons of men to be afflicted with.”

But he does not stop at the burden. A few lines later he says, “He has made everything beautiful in its time.” In the same breath he says that God “has also set eternity in their hearts”, and that people still cannot find out the whole of what God has done. And he draws a plain conclusion: “there is nothing better for them than to rejoice, and to do good as long as they live.”
around:
The book opens with its speaker: “The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem”. He asks early on what a person gains from all labor under the sun, and the poem of the seasons answers that question only partway. Later in chapter 3 he looks at the place of justice and sees wickedness there, and says in his heart that God will judge the righteous and the wicked, because there is a time for every purpose and for every work.

The book ends by looking back at all of it: “Fear God and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man.”
after:
In the Bible, the Preacher’s own answer comes at the end of the book. After everything has been heard, he says to fear God and keep his commandments, and that God will bring every work into judgment. The poem of the seasons is not the last word of the book. It is one stop on a long road of thought.

In Jewish life Ecclesiastes is read in the synagogue on the Shabbat of Sukkot. The tradition ascribes it to King Solomon, though most biblical scholars question that.

The poem itself reached a very wide audience through Pete Seeger’s song. Judy Collins recorded it in 1963, and The Byrds took it to the top of the American charts in the winter of 1965. Stereogum notes that almost all the words of the song come straight from the King James translation of the Bible. So the old words of Ecclesiastes came back into the popular music of the 1960s.
readings:
Some readers hear the poem as comfort. If there is a season for everything, then grief and joy are both part of a life that is held by someone. On this reading the verses that follow, “He has made everything beautiful in its time”, are the heart of the passage.

Others hear a more somber note. The Preacher says that “for all is vanity”, that all go to one place, and that no one can find out the work that God has done from the beginning to the end. On this reading the poem is not a promise that things will turn out well. It says that we do not control the timing.

A third group looks at the question that follows, “What profit has he who works in that in which he labors?” They read the poem as the reason that question hurts: if every season passes, what lasts? The book does not hand over a single easy answer, and My Jewish Learning notes that the traditional author, Solomon, is not uniformly pessimistic.
argued: Readers have long argued about who spoke these words. The book presents its speaker as the son of David and king in Jerusalem, and the traditional rabbinic and early Christian view assigned it to Solomon. Many modern critical scholars have given that view up, and New World Encyclopedia says there is no scholarly consensus on the date, with proposals running from the fourth to the second century BCE. They also disagree about what the speaker’s title, Qoheleth, means: the one who gathers, or the one among the gathering.
point: The verse is not a slogan about taking things as they come. It opens a list of fourteen pairs that the Preacher sets down before asking what profit anyone has in labor, and then answers that God has made everything beautiful in its time. The song carried it into the Vietnam era. The book places it inside a much larger question.
lesson:
You may be in a season right now that you did not choose. The poem does not tell you to like it, and it does not say it will pass quickly. It says only that it is a season, one of many, and that your life has room for both the weeping and the laughing.

If you are in a time of grief, you do not need to hurry through it. There is a time to mourn, and the Preacher puts it right beside a time to dance. If you are in a good time, the Preacher says to rejoice and to do good while you can.

You are invited to read the rest of the chapter, not just the famous lines. It asks honest questions, and it lets you ask them too. And if you do not share this faith, the poem still holds something true for anyone: that no season is the whole of a life.

echoes.note: A psalmist surrounded by enemies prays, “My times are in your hand.” The seasons of life are not left to chance but are held by God.
The prayer asks, “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” Like the Preacher, it ties wisdom to knowing that our time is short.
In Babylon, Daniel praises God: “He changes the times and the seasons.” The Preacher’s idea of timing is told here from a king’s court.
